concept.title: Cascade and declarations
concept.shortdesc: CSS rules associate selectors with declarations. A declaration has a property name, a colon, a value and a semicolon:

conbody.p: The cascade is the process that decides which declaration sets a property on an element when several declarations apply to it. It compares the declarations one criterion at a time and keeps the winner.
For each element and property, the cascade chooses among the declarations that apply. It does not choose one declaration for an entire rule. One rule can win for color while another wins for margin.

section.title: From a declaration to a value
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §4, Value Processing; CSS Cascade 5 §5, Filtering.
CSS processes a property through several value stages:

ol.li: A declared value is the value written in a declaration.
A cascaded value is the result of comparing the applicable declarations.
A specified value resolves CSS-wide keywords and uses inheritance or the property’s initial value when needed.
A computed value resolves values that can be determined without knowing the final layout.
A used value incorporates information available during layout.
An actual value is the value that can be represented in the output medium.

section.p: The cascade concerns the first two stages. Inheritance and defaulting follow the cascade. Computation and layout follow those stages.

Declarations are filtered before they compete. A rule must apply to the element, its selector must match, and its enclosing conditions must hold. A declaration with an unknown property or invalid value does not provide a candidate. A value that becomes invalid only after substitution is different: it fails after the cascade has already chosen it. See Inheritance and default values and Custom properties and substitution.
CSSMedia processes declarations from its user-agent rules and author stylesheets. The cascade guides explain the CSS rules used to select values from those declarations.

ul.li: Cascade order and layers: importance, origins, layers, specificity, scope proximity and source order.
